answer:
An ETF’s quoted spread reflects the cost and risk of providing immediacy—not just trading the ETF. If its holdings are costly or difficult to trade due to wide spreads, shallow depth, market closures, or volatility, market makers face greater hedging costs and uncertainty, so they may quote wider. Using correlated instruments can help when direct hedging is impractical, but adds basis and execution risk.

Creation and redemption help align ETF prices with portfolio value, but basket trading, financing, fees, operational constraints, and inventory risk make arbitrage imperfect and can affect quotes.

Historical exchange volume measures past ETF trading, not current order-book depth, underlying liquidity, or dealers’ ability to hedge and process baskets. A lightly traded ETF can still have competitive quotes if its holdings and hedges are liquid; high volume alone doesn’t ensure tight spreads.

An ETF’s quoted spread reflects the cost and risk of providing immediacy, not just trading in the ETF itself. When underlying holdings are costly or difficult to trade—because of wide spreads, low depth, market closures, or volatility—market makers face higher costs and uncertainty when hedging, and may quote wider. They may hedge with correlated instruments when direct trading is impractical, but basis risk and hedge execution costs also matter.

Creation and redemption can help align ETF prices with portfolio value, but they are not frictionless: basket trading, financing, fees, operational constraints, and inventory risk affect the arbitrage channel and can feed into quotes.

Historical exchange volume captures past ETF trading, not current order-book depth, the liquidity of the holdings, or how easily dealers can hedge and process baskets. A lightly traded ETF can still have competitive quotes when its holdings and hedges are liquid; high volume alone does not guarantee tight quotes.
